summary: Surveys commonly used network security protocols, looking at how they interact with applications and transport protocols. It supplements work to define and catalog Transport Services by describing the interfaces needed to add security protocols. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Secure connections are built from layers that must fit together. This document looks at how popular security tools plug into the layers below and above them, to help design a common way to use them.

subtitle: How security protocols fit with transport layers and applications

tldr.problem: Building secure connections requires multiple protocols that must work together, but different security protocols have different requirements and interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: This survey catalogs commonly used security protocols like TLS, DTLS, QUIC, IPsec, and WireGuard, showing how each one connects to transport protocols and applications.
tldr.outcome: The taxonomy helps design systems that can support multiple security protocols through a common interface, improving flexibility and interoperability.

today: RFC 8922 is an Informational document published in October 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so the survey remains the current reference for understanding how security protocols interface with transport and applications.

sections.title: Security Protocols and Transport Services
sections.content:
Network security relies on multiple layers of protocols working together. This RFC surveys the most commonly used and notable security protocols, examining how they interact with both the transport protocols below them and the applications above them.

The survey covers a superset of functionality that any Transport Services system might need to support, including IETF standards like TLS and DTLS, newer protocols like QUIC and WireGuard, and specialized protocols like tcpcrypt. The goal is to identify common interface surfaces so that applications can switch between different security protocols without rewriting their code, as long as those protocols provide similar feature sets.
sections.eli5: When you build something from parts, you want to know which parts fit together. This document maps out the popular security tools so you can understand how they connect to each other.

sections.title: Categories of Security Protocols
sections.content:
Security protocols fit into four main categories based on what they protect and where they sit in the stack.

Application Payload Security Protocols like TLS and DTLS protect just the application data, not the transport headers. Application-Specific Security Protocols like Secure RTP (SRTP) are designed for particular use cases and require a separate handshake protocol. Transport-Layer Security Protocols like QUIC and tcpcrypt protect both the application data and the transport headers. Packet Security Protocols like IPsec and WireGuard protect entire IP packets and are typically used for tunnels or VPNs.

Each protocol can be understood in terms of two components: a handshake protocol that negotiates parameters and establishes keys, and a record protocol that encrypts the traffic using those keys. In some protocols like TLS these are tightly integrated, while in others like IPsec they are separated.
sections.eli5: There are four kinds of security tools. Some protect just your message, some work only for certain kinds of messages, some protect both your message and the delivery instructions, and some protect entire packages as they travel.

sections.title: What Transport Protocols Are Needed
sections.content:
Different security protocols have different requirements from the transport layer below them.

Some protocols like TLS and tcpcrypt require a reliable byte-stream transport. They expect the transport to deliver every byte in order with no gaps or duplicates. Typically these run over TCP.

Other protocols like DTLS, QUIC, IPsec, WireGuard, and MinimaLT work with unreliable datagram transports like UDP. They do not depend on the transport for reliability, so they can send individual messages that may be lost or arrive out of order.

Some datagram protocols also define how to run over TCP if needed. For example, DTLS can be used to establish keys for SRTP over a TCP connection, and IPsec can be tunneled through TCP.
sections.eli5: Some security tools need delivery that guarantees every piece arrives in order, like mail with a signature. Others are okay with individual messages that might not arrive, like postcards.

sections.title: How Applications Use Security Protocols
sections.content:
All security protocols expose interfaces to applications, but not all protocols expose all interfaces. These interfaces are grouped into three phases.

Pre-connection interfaces configure the protocol before a handshake starts. They let applications supply identity and private keys, choose cryptographic algorithms, configure extensions like ALPN, save and resume sessions, use pre-shared keys, or delegate authentication.

Connection interfaces happen during the handshake. The protocol validates the peer's identity, may perform source address validation to prevent denial-of-service attacks, and exchanges authenticated handshake messages with the application.

Post-connection interfaces manage the ongoing session. Applications can signal connection termination, request key updates, extract shared secrets for application-specific uses, or signal mobility events when the connection changes transport paths or addresses.

Different protocols expose different subsets of these interfaces. For example, TLS exposes most interfaces but not mobility events, while WireGuard exposes fewer interfaces because it uses pre-shared keys and offers no negotiation or algorithmic agility.
sections.eli5: When you make a secure connection, you set it up, use it, and then close it. Each step has options. Some tools let you control all the options, while others make simpler choices for you.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Properties
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that this survey catalogs existing protocols but does not recommend specific ones for particular uses. All the surveyed protocols improve privacy by encrypting data, but they handle metadata differently.

Applications using security protocols should be aware of limitations beyond what the protocol itself guarantees. For example, timing side channels and traffic analysis may leak information even when data is encrypted. Additionally, different versions of the same protocol have different security guarantees; TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 differ in how they handle certificate encryption. The survey notes that these variations mean implementations must only use protocols and algorithms explicitly requested by applications or required by system policy; automatic protocol switching is not appropriate.
sections.eli5: Encryption keeps your message secret, but it might not hide that you sent it, or how often, or how long your message was. Different tools hide different amounts of information.
